@Component.summary: @Component marks a TypeScript class as an Angular component. Its metadata defines the selector, rendered template, and optional styles.
@Component.explanation: The @Component decorator adds Angular metadata to a TypeScript class. The metadata tells Angular which HTML selector uses the component, what template it renders, and optionally which styles apply to its template. Templates and styles can also be stored in separate files.
@Component.syntax:
@Component({ selector: string, template?: string, templateUrl?: string, styles?: string | string[], styleUrl?: string, imports?: Array<any> })
export class ComponentName {}

parameters.name: selector
parameters.description: HTML name or selector pattern used to place the component.

parameters.name: template
parameters.description: Inline HTML template rendered by the component.

parameters.name: templateUrl
parameters.description: Path to an external HTML template, relative to the component directory.

parameters.name: styles
parameters.description: Inline CSS applied to the component template.

parameters.name: styleUrl
parameters.description: Path to an external CSS file, relative to the component directory.

@Component.returns: A decorated TypeScript class that Angular treats as a component.

example.title: A component with inline template and styles
example.explanation: This component uses an inline template and inline CSS. Angular matches it with the profile-photo element.

useCases.title: Reusable UI parts
useCases.scenario: A component renders a small reusable part of a page, such as a profile image.

useCases.title: Interactive behavior
useCases.scenario: A component needs behavior for user actions and data loading.

useCases.title: Separate presentation files
useCases.scenario: A project keeps HTML and CSS outside TypeScript files.

interview.question: What are the basic parts of an Angular component?
interview.answer: A component needs a TypeScript class, an HTML template, and a CSS selector. The @Component decorator connects these parts through metadata.
interview.followUp: How can the template and styles be moved out of the class? Use templateUrl and styleUrl, with paths relative to the component's directory.

interview.question: What does the metadata in @Component describe?
interview.answer: The selector defines the HTML form used to place the component. The template controls what Angular renders into the DOM, while the class supplies behavior such as input handling or data fetching.
interview.followUp: What controls the component's visual appearance? The styles or styleUrl metadata property supplies CSS for the component.

interview.question: How do you make another component available in a component template?
interview.answer: Add the component, directive, or pipe to the imports array in the @Component decorator before using it in that component's template. This makes the referenced item available to the template.
interview.followUp: Where are imported template dependencies declared? In the imports property of the component whose template uses them.

keyPoints: The class contains component behavior, such as responding to user input or fetching server data.
The template determines the DOM content rendered by the component.
The selector determines how the component appears in HTML.
The decorator object is metadata that describes the component.
Use templateUrl and styleUrl when presentation files should be separate from the TypeScript class.
Relative paths for external templates and styles start from the component's directory.
gotchas: Styles declared by a component do not normally affect elements outside that component's template.
A component, directive, or pipe used in the template must be listed in the component's imports array.

@defer.summary: @defer lazy-loads template dependencies that are not needed for the first render. It supports triggers, prefetching, and placeholder, loading, and error states.
@defer.explanation: Angular uses @defer to split selected template dependencies into separately loaded code. The deferred content appears after its trigger fires or its when condition becomes true. Optional placeholder, loading, and error blocks handle the other states.
@defer.syntax: @defer (on <trigger>; when <condition>; prefetch on <trigger>; prefetch when <condition>) { ... } @placeholder (minimum? <duration>) { ... } @loading (minimum? <duration>; after? <duration>) { ... } @error { ... }

example.title: Defer a component until interaction
example.explanation: Angular loads the component when the placeholder is interacted with. It can fetch the code earlier when the browser is idle.

useCases.title: Delay secondary UI
useCases.scenario: Load a large component only after a user opens or interacts with its placeholder.

useCases.title: Viewport-based loading
useCases.scenario: Load content when it becomes visible on screen.

useCases.title: Prefetch before use
useCases.scenario: Fetch deferred code during idle time but wait to render it until a later event.

useCases.title: Handle loading states
useCases.scenario: Show stable placeholder and loading states while a network request loads deferred code.

interview.question: What does @defer do?
interview.answer: @defer delays loading components, directives, and pipes inside its main block. Angular creates dynamic imports for those dependencies, and renders the block after the imports finish.
interview.followUp: What must be true for a dependency to be deferred? The dependency must be standalone and must not be referenced outside the defer block in the same file.

interview.question: Which triggers can start a defer block?
interview.answer: The on trigger controls when Angular loads and displays the block. Available triggers include idle, viewport, interaction, hover, immediate, and timer; when uses a custom truthy condition.
interview.followUp: How do multiple triggers behave? They are separated with semicolons and act as OR conditions.

interview.question: How do the optional blocks work?
interview.answer: @placeholder shows before loading starts, @loading shows while deferred dependencies load, and @error shows if loading fails. These optional blocks are eagerly loaded.
interview.followUp: How can flicker be reduced? Use minimum on placeholder or loading, and use after on loading to delay its display.

keyPoints: Use @defer to lazy-load components, directives, and pipes from a template.
Without a trigger, Angular starts loading when the browser is idle.
The placeholder is replaced by deferred content after loading finishes.
Use when with a condition to start loading when that expression becomes truthy.
The viewport trigger starts loading when the watched content enters the viewport.
The interaction trigger responds to user interaction with the placeholder or a referenced element.
gotchas: Dependencies must be standalone to be deferred. Non-standalone dependencies load eagerly even when placed inside @defer.
A dependency used elsewhere in the same file, including in a ViewChild query, is loaded eagerly.

@for.summary: The Angular @for block renders a template for each item in a collection. It requires track to identify items and can show @empty content when the collection has no items.
@for.explanation: The @for block creates content for every value in a JavaScript iterable. Angular uses the track expression to match items with existing DOM views, so it can update only the needed views when the collection changes. An optional @empty block renders when there are no items.

example.title: Render a list
example.explanation: This renders one list item for each item and shows a fallback when the collection is empty.

useCases.title: Render collections
useCases.scenario: Display rows, cards, or list items from an array or other iterable.

useCases.title: Handle empty collections
useCases.scenario: Show a message or placeholder when a collection has no values.

useCases.title: Update changing lists
useCases.scenario: Keep DOM updates small when items are inserted, removed, or moved.

interview.question: What does @for do?
interview.answer: @for repeats its block for each item in a collection. The collection can be any JavaScript iterable, although arrays can provide performance benefits.
interview.followUp: What lets Angular reduce DOM work? The track expression supplies an identity key that Angular uses to associate items with DOM views.

interview.question: Why is track required, and how should it be chosen?
interview.answer: The track expression identifies each item for DOM reconciliation. Use a unique item property for collections that can be added to, removed from, or reordered.
interview.followUp: What should be used for a fixed collection? track $index is a simple option when the collection does not change.

interview.question: Which contextual variables are available?
interview.answer: @for provides implicit variables such as $count, $index, $first, $last, $even, and $odd. These values describe the collection and the current row.
interview.followUp: How can an implicit variable be renamed? Use a let segment to create an alias, such as let i = $index.

keyPoints: Angular re-renders the block as the collection changes.
Any JavaScript iterable can be used, but arrays may perform better.
An @empty section can provide empty-state content.
track supplies the key that connects items to DOM views.
The block exposes implicit context values, including the collection count.
gotchas: Do not use continue or break inside the block.
A track expression is required.
Using $index is suited to static collections, not changing ones.

@HostListener.summary: @HostListener connects a class method to a DOM event on the host element. It can also listen on document, window, or body and pass event values to the method.
@HostListener.explanation: Apply @HostListener to a class method to register a DOM event handler. Angular calls the method when the host element, or a named global target, emits the event. The optional argument list supplies values such as the event object. Returning false makes Angular prevent the event's default action.

parameters.name: eventName
parameters.description: The DOM event name. It may include a global target prefix or keyboard modifiers.

parameters.name: args
parameters.description: Optional expressions whose values are passed to the handler method.

example.title: Listen for a global key event
example.explanation: This component listens for Enter on the global window and increases the count.

useCases.title: Handle host-element events
useCases.scenario: A directive needs to react when its host element is clicked.

useCases.title: Handle global keyboard events
useCases.scenario: A component must respond to a key press on the browser window.

useCases.title: Pass event data to a method
useCases.scenario: A handler needs the event target or full event object.

interview.question: What does @HostListener do?
interview.answer: @HostListener decorates a method and declares the DOM event that should call it. Angular can pass values such as $event through the optional argument array.
interview.followUp: How can a handler stop the default action? If the handler returns false, Angular applies preventDefault to the bound element.

interview.question: How do you listen for global or keyboard events?
interview.answer: The event name can start with window:, document:, or body:. For example, window:keydown.enter listens for Enter on the global window.
interview.followUp: How do you match a physical key instead of a layout-dependent key? Use a code modifier such as keydown.code.KeyA.

interview.question: What are the arguments to the decorator?
interview.answer: The first argument is the event name. The second is an optional string array containing expressions such as $event.target or $event.
interview.followUp: What happens when the method returns false? Angular applies preventDefault to the bound element.

keyPoints: Use the decorator to connect a DOM event to a class method.
The default listener is attached to the host element of the directive or component.
Angular uses the handler result when updating the bound element.
Returning false requests default-action prevention.
Provide the event name and, when needed, expressions that supply method arguments.
gotchas: Prefer the component or directive's host property for new code. @HostListener remains for backwards compatibility.
A named key such as Enter follows the keyboard layout. Use a code modifier when you need to identify the physical key.
Only document, window, and body are documented as global event targets.

@if.summary: `@if` conditionally renders template content when its condition is truthy. It also supports `@else if`, `@else`, and local names for expression results.
@if.explanation: Angular evaluates the condition in an `@if` block. It adds the block's content to the DOM when the result is truthy and removes it when the result is not. You can add `@else if` and `@else` blocks, and bind an expression result to a local name with `as`.

example.title: Display content conditionally
example.explanation: This template stores the async result in `users` and shows a different message when the condition is false.

useCases.title: Conditional content
useCases.scenario: Show a section only when a Boolean or comparison expression is truthy.

useCases.title: Multiple conditions
useCases.scenario: Choose one of several template branches.

useCases.title: Named expression result
useCases.scenario: Reuse an async or computed expression inside a block.

interview.question: What does `@if` do?
interview.answer: `@if` conditionally renders template content. Angular adds the content when the condition is truthy and removes it otherwise.
interview.followUp: How can a template use the result of an expression? Use the `as` clause to assign the result to a local template variable.

interview.question: How do `@else if` and `@else` work with `@if`?
interview.answer: Use `@else if` for another condition and `@else` for the fallback case. These blocks form one conditional structure.
interview.followUp: What happens when no condition is truthy? The `@else` content is rendered when it exists; otherwise, no branch content is shown.

interview.question: How can `@if` expose an expression result inside its block?
interview.answer: The block supports binding an expression result with `as`, such as `@if (users$ | async; as users)`. The local name can then be used inside the block.
interview.followUp: Why is this useful? It lets the template reuse the evaluated result, such as reading `users.length`, instead of repeating the expression.

keyPoints: Use `@if` when content should appear only for a truthy condition.
An `@if` chain can test another condition with `@else if`.
Add `@else` to provide content when earlier conditions do not match.
The block can expose an expression result for reuse inside its content.
gotchas: The block changes the DOM. Content is not merely hidden with CSS.

@Injectable.summary: @Injectable marks a class so Angular can generate the metadata needed to create its dependencies during injection. Its options can define the injector scope for the provider.
@Injectable.explanation: @Injectable marks a class so Angular's compiler can generate the metadata needed to create that class's dependencies when it is injected. It can also accept options that set where a provider is available, such as the root injector or platform injector.
@Injectable.syntax:
@Injectable(options?: { providedIn: Type<any> | 'any' } & InjectableProvider);
@Injectable(options?: { providedIn: 'root' | 'platform' | null } & InjectableProvider);

parameters.name: options
parameters.type: { providedIn: Type<any> | 'any' } & InjectableProvider | { providedIn: 'root' | 'platform' | null } & InjectableProvider
parameters.description: Optional configuration for the injectable provider, including the injector scope.

@Injectable.returns: A class decorator that marks a class for dependency injection.

example.title: Mark classes for dependency injection
example.explanation: The decorator marks both classes so Angular can create the dependency when it creates NeedsService.

useCases.title: Declare constructor dependencies
useCases.scenario: A service constructor needs another service.

useCases.title: Enable dependency injection
useCases.scenario: A class must be created by an Angular injector.

useCases.title: Configure provider availability
useCases.scenario: A provider needs an explicit injector scope.

interview.question: What does @Injectable do?
interview.answer: @Injectable tells Angular's compiler to generate metadata needed to create a class's dependencies during injection. A class can then be constructed by an injector with its required services.
interview.followUp: What happens when a class has no dependencies? The decorator can still mark it for injection, and the injector can create it with no dependency list.

interview.question: What options can @Injectable accept?
interview.answer: The decorator accepts an options object. Its providedIn value can describe the injector scope, including root, platform, or null, depending on the supported signature.
interview.followUp: Why use providedIn? It declares where the service is provided instead of requiring the provider to be listed separately in every injector configuration.

interview.question: How does an injector use an injectable class with a constructor dependency?
interview.answer: The documented example marks both the service and the class that receives it with @Injectable. The injector then creates NeedsService and supplies a UsefulService instance to its constructor.
interview.followUp: How can the injector be configured explicitly? Use Injector.create with provider entries and dependency lists, as shown in the documentation.

keyPoints: @Injectable marks a class for compiler-generated dependency metadata.
The metadata lets Angular create the class's dependencies when an injector requests the class.
A service with constructor dependencies should be marked with the decorator.
A supporting service can then be supplied while the dependent class is created.
gotchas: Use the decorator on a class that has dependencies so the compiler can generate the metadata required for injection.

@Input.sourceTitle: Accepting data with input properties • Angular
@Input.summary: @Input exposes a component property for parent-to-child binding. Its options can require a value, transform incoming data, or provide a template alias.
@Input.explanation: The @Input decorator makes a component property available for parent-to-child binding. Its configuration can require a value, transform incoming data, or give the template a different name.

example.title: Decorator input with alias
example.explanation: The component declares a required input named value and exposes it in templates as sliderValue.

useCases.title: Receive component data
useCases.scenario: A parent component passes a value to a child component.

useCases.title: Require an input
useCases.scenario: A component must reject uses that omit a needed value.

useCases.title: Transform input values
useCases.scenario: Incoming text or other data needs normalization before use.

useCases.title: Alias an input
useCases.scenario: A public template name should differ from the class property name.

interview.question: What does @Input do?
interview.answer: The @Input decorator exposes a component property for template binding. A parent can set it with property binding, such as [value]="50".
interview.followUp: How can the template name differ from the class property? Use the alias option, such as @Input({alias: 'sliderValue'}) value = 0.

interview.question: How do you make an input required?
interview.answer: Set required to true in the decorator configuration. Angular then reports a build-time error when a component use does not provide that input.
interview.followUp: Can a required input also have a template alias? Yes. The configuration can include both required: true and alias.

interview.question: When would you use an input transform?
interview.answer: The transform option runs when Angular sets the input value. It can normalize or convert the incoming value before the component uses it.
interview.followUp: What should replace a setter when only input conversion is needed? Prefer an input transform instead of a getter or setter.

keyPoints: Use a configuration object to customize an input.
An alias changes the name that templates use for the input.
A transform changes the value when Angular sets the input.
The component decorator can list inherited properties as inputs.
gotchas: Do not put expensive work in an input setter. Angular can call the setter more than once, which can hurt performance.
A required input must be supplied wherever the component is used.
Choose names that do not conflict with native element properties.

@NgModule.summary: NgModule is a decorator for defining an Angular module class. It describes the declarations, imports, providers, and optional bootstrap components used by that module.
@NgModule.explanation: NgModule is a decorator for defining an Angular module class. Its metadata describes the components, directives, pipes, imports, providers, and optional bootstrap components that Angular uses for compilation and dependency injection.
@NgModule.syntax:
@NgModule({ declarations: [], imports: [], providers: [], bootstrap: [] })
export class FeatureModule {}

parameters.name: metadata
parameters.description: Metadata describing declarations, imports, providers, and optional bootstrap components.

example.title: Basic NgModule
example.explanation: This module declares the application component, imports another module, and identifies the component to render when the application starts.

useCases.title: Organize an existing application
useCases.scenario: Existing module-based applications need a central place to register declarations and imports.

useCases.title: Provide dependencies
useCases.scenario: A module supplies injectable services for components, directives, and pipes that import it.

useCases.title: Bootstrap an application
useCases.scenario: A module-based application needs to identify its root component and start with bootstrapModule.

interview.question: What is NgModule?
interview.answer: NgModule is a class with the NgModule decorator. The decorator metadata tells Angular which declarations belong to the module and how dependency injection is configured.
interview.followUp: What can an NgModule declare? It can declare components, directives, and pipes, and the declarations can include nested arrays.

interview.question: What is the purpose of declarations?
interview.answer: The declarations array lists the components, directives, and pipes owned by the module. A declaration must not appear in more than one NgModule.
interview.followUp: What must a declaration have in current Angular? It must be explicitly marked standalone: false.

interview.question: How does an NgModule application start?
interview.answer: The bootstrap array names the component or components that start the application. bootstrapModule starts the NgModule application, and Angular renders the bootstrapped component using its CSS selector.
interview.followUp: What happens to providers during NgModule bootstrapping? Providers from the module and its imports are eagerly loaded and available throughout the application.

keyPoints: The decorator metadata controls template compilation and dependency injection.
Use declarations to list the components, directives, and pipes owned by the module.
Declarations may contain nested arrays, so shared declaration lists can be reused.
An NgModule can add providers to the injector used by code that imports it.
Use bootstrapModule from platformBrowser or platformServer to start a module-based application.
gotchas: A component, directive, or pipe must use standalone: false before an NgModule can declare it.
Do not declare the same component, directive, or pipe in multiple NgModules.
NgModule is mainly useful when working with existing module-based applications; new code should generally use standalone components.

@Output.summary: `@Output` marks a component property as a custom event. Parent templates can listen to the event, and an `EventEmitter` sends it with `emit`.
@Output.explanation: `@Output` marks a property as a custom event that a parent component can listen to in its template. The property is commonly an `EventEmitter`, and code sends the event by calling `emit`; an alias can give the event a different template name.

parameters.name: alias
parameters.description: Optional template name for the output event. The TypeScript property name remains unchanged.

@Output.returns: A decorator that marks a property as a component output.

example.title: Declare and emit a component output
example.explanation: The component declares an output and emits it when `close` runs. A parent template can listen to the event by using the output name.

useCases.title: Notify a parent
useCases.scenario: A child component needs to notify its parent that an action finished.

useCases.title: Use an event alias
useCases.scenario: A component should expose a public event name that differs from its TypeScript property name.

useCases.title: Expose an inherited output
useCases.scenario: A child class inherits an output from a base component.

interview.question: What does `@Output` do?
interview.answer: `@Output` declares a component property as a custom event. A parent can listen to that event in its template, and an `EventEmitter` can send it with `emit`.
interview.followUp: Can the template event name differ from the property name? Yes. Pass an alias to `@Output`; TypeScript still uses the original property name.

interview.question: How do you declare an output with the decorator API?
interview.answer: Create an `EventEmitter` property and decorate it with `@Output`. Give the emitter a type that matches the value the component will emit, such as `void` or `number`.
interview.followUp: How can a component emit no payload? Use `EventEmitter<void>` and call `emit()` without an argument.

interview.question: How can component metadata declare outputs?
interview.answer: The `outputs` component metadata can list an inherited output property. It can also map a property to a template alias by using the form `property: alias`.
interview.followUp: Why is metadata useful with inheritance? It lets the child component expose an output inherited from its base class.

keyPoints: The decorator API is still supported, although Angular recommends the output function for new projects.
Send an output event by calling `emit` on its `EventEmitter`.
Pass a string to `@Output` to give the event a different template name.
gotchas: Use camelCase for output names. Do not add an `on` prefix.
An alias changes the event name used in templates, but the TypeScript property keeps its original name.
Do not prefix output names as if they were component selectors.

@switch.summary: @switch chooses which template block to render by comparing one condition with @case values. It uses strict equality, supports grouped cases, and can check union cases for completeness.
@switch.explanation: Use @switch to choose one template block from several cases. Angular compares the condition with each case using strict equality. It can group cases, has no fallthrough, and may include an optional default block.

parameters.name: condition
parameters.description: The expression whose value Angular compares with each case expression.

example.title: Render content by state
example.explanation: The block renders the content whose case equals currentState. The default content handles every other value.

useCases.title: State-based UI
useCases.scenario: Show different controls for states such as logged in, logged out, or loading.

useCases.title: Grouped alternatives
useCases.scenario: Display one view for several equivalent values by placing consecutive cases before it.

useCases.title: Exhaustive union handling
useCases.scenario: Verify that every member of a TypeScript union has a template branch.

interview.question: How does @switch choose a case?
interview.answer: @switch selects content by comparing its condition with each @case using the === operator. The first matching case determines the rendered block.
interview.followUp: How can a template handle several values with one block? Put consecutive @case statements before that block; Angular treats them as alternative conditions without fallthrough.

interview.question: Is @default required?
interview.answer: The @default block is optional. If no case matches and there is no default, Angular shows nothing.
interview.followUp: What happens when a default block contains never? It asks the template type checker to verify that no union members remain uncovered.

interview.question: How does exhaustive type checking work?
interview.answer: For exhaustive checking, use a variable with a union type and write @default never;. Angular can then report an error when a later union member has no case.
interview.followUp: Why might @default never fail to check a signal? TypeScript narrowing used by this feature works on variables, so first assign the signal value to @let.

keyPoints: @switch renders the block selected by the matching case.
Case matching uses strict equality.
Several consecutive cases can share one block.
A matched case does not continue into the next case.
You may leave out the default block.
A union type can be checked for missing cases at compile time.
gotchas: Exhaustive checking does not work directly with a function call or signal expression.
Assign a signal result to a @let variable before using it as the switch condition.
Without a matching case or default block, Angular renders no content.

@ViewChild.summary: @ViewChild finds the first matching item in a component's view and assigns it to a class property. It supports components, directives, template references, providers, string tokens, and templates.
@ViewChild.explanation: @ViewChild finds one item in a component's view and assigns the result to a class property. It can query a component, directive, template reference, provider, or template, and can read another supported token from the match.

parameters.name: selector
parameters.description: The directive type, template reference name, provider token, string token, or TemplateRef to find.

parameters.name: read
parameters.description: An optional token to return from the matched element.

parameters.name: static
parameters.description: Whether to resolve before change detection and never update later. Defaults to false.

@ViewChild.returns: A property decorator that creates a view query and assigns the first matching result to the decorated property or setter.

example.title: Query a view element
example.explanation: The query finds the button by its template reference name. Angular assigns the matching result to the class property.

useCases.title: Access a child component or directive
useCases.scenario: Get a component or directive instance from the current component's template.

useCases.title: Read a view reference
useCases.scenario: Get a template reference by its name, such as #input.

useCases.title: Read another token
useCases.scenario: Retrieve a framework token or provider from a matched element.

useCases.title: Query a template
useCases.scenario: Find an ng-template for later template operations.

interview.question: What does @ViewChild do, and what can it query?
interview.answer: @ViewChild queries the current component's view and stores the first matching result in a property. The selector may be a component or directive type, a template reference string, a provider, or TemplateRef.
interview.followUp: How can the returned value differ from the matched object? Use the read option to request a supported token such as ElementRef, TemplateRef, ViewContainerRef, or Injector.

interview.question: What is the difference between dynamic and static queries?
interview.answer: By default, the query is dynamic because static defaults to false. It resolves before ngAfterViewInit and updates when view blocks such as conditional or repeated content change.
interview.followUp: When would static: true be appropriate? When the target exists when the view is created and must be available before change detection; it will not track later view changes.

interview.question: What is the purpose of the read option?
interview.answer: The selector identifies what to match, while read chooses what token to return from the matched element. The read token can be a component or directive class, an injector provider, a string provider token, or one of the supported framework tokens.
interview.followUp: Can read select any arbitrary value? No. It must be a supported token available from the matched element's injector or one of the listed framework tokens.

keyPoints: selector tells Angular what to find. It can be a class, a template reference name, a provider, a string token, or TemplateRef.
read lets the query return a different supported token from the matched element instead of the default result.
static is false unless set otherwise, so most queries are dynamic.
A provider query can find a provider in the child component tree.
TemplateRef can be used as the selector to find an ng-template.
read supports TemplateRef, ElementRef, ViewContainerRef, and Injector, along with supported classes and providers.
gotchas: The default dynamic query can change when the view changes. A static query does not update after the view is created.
A static query is available before change detection and before ngOnInit, while a dynamic query resolves before ngAfterViewInit.

ActivatedRoute.summary: ActivatedRoute lets a routed component read its route information. It provides observables for URL parts, parameters, fragments, titles, and route data, plus links for walking the router state tree.
ActivatedRoute.explanation: ActivatedRoute gives a component access to information for the route that loaded it. It exposes observables for URL segments, route parameters, query parameters, the fragment, title, and static or resolved data. It also provides links for walking through the router state tree, plus snapshot and parameter-map forms.

example.title: Read a route parameter
example.explanation: This component reads the route parameter named id as an observable.

useCases.title: Read route parameters
useCases.scenario: A component needs an ID from its route.

useCases.title: Read query parameters
useCases.scenario: A page filters or changes state using URL query values.

useCases.title: Read resolved data
useCases.scenario: A component needs data loaded by a resolver.

useCases.title: Traverse route state
useCases.scenario: A component needs to inspect related route levels.

interview.question: What is ActivatedRoute used for?
interview.answer: ActivatedRoute represents the route associated with a component in an outlet. It provides route information through observables such as params, queryParams, url, fragment, and data.
interview.followUp: How can the component inspect the route tree? Use root, parent, firstChild, children, and pathFromRoot to move through related route nodes.

interview.question: How do route and query parameters differ?
interview.answer: Use params for matrix parameters scoped to the current route and queryParams for query parameters shared by all routes. Use paramMap and queryParamMap when a map-style parameter API is preferred.
interview.followUp: Why might query parameters be available on several route nodes? They are shared by all routes, unlike matrix parameters, which belong to a route segment.

interview.question: When should snapshot be used instead of an observable?
interview.answer: snapshot contains the current ActivatedRouteSnapshot and gives a non-observable view of the route at that point. The observable properties are useful when route values can change while the component remains active.
interview.followUp: What data does data expose? It combines static route data with resolved route data, so consumers can read both through the same observable.

keyPoints: Inject ActivatedRoute in a routed component to read information about the route that loaded it.
The route exposes navigation through the router-state tree, including parent, child, root, and path-from-root relationships.
url emits the URL segments matched by the current route.
params contains matrix parameters that belong to the current route.
queryParams provides query parameters shared across the route tree.
data combines static route data and values produced by route resolvers.
gotchas: Route observables use shallow equality. A deep change inside resolved data might not produce a new data emission.

AsyncPipe.summary: AsyncPipe displays the latest value from an Observable or Promise in an Angular template. It updates the component when values arrive and cleans up subscriptions automatically.
AsyncPipe.explanation: AsyncPipe connects an Observable or Promise to an Angular template. It displays the latest value, asks Angular to check the component when that value changes, and manages subscription cleanup when the component is destroyed or the input reference changes.

parameters.name: ref
parameters.description: The ChangeDetectorRef used by the pipe to request component checking when the asynchronous value changes.

parameters.name: obj
parameters.description: An Observable, Promise, or null or undefined input to transform.

AsyncPipe.returns: The latest value from the Observable or Promise, typed as T | null; null or undefined input returns null.

example.title: Display an Observable value
example.explanation: The pipe subscribes to the Observable and displays its latest emitted value.

useCases.title: Show Observable data
useCases.scenario: A component has an Observable that provides data for its template.

useCases.title: Show a Promise result
useCases.scenario: A component waits for a Promise to resolve before displaying its result.

useCases.title: Switch asynchronous sources
useCases.scenario: A template source can change during the component's lifetime.

interview.question: What does AsyncPipe do?
interview.answer: AsyncPipe accepts an Observable or Promise and returns its latest emitted or resolved value. It also marks the component for change detection when a new value arrives.
interview.followUp: What happens when the bound source changes? AsyncPipe unsubscribes from the old source and subscribes to the new one.

interview.question: How does AsyncPipe handle cleanup?
interview.answer: It unsubscribes automatically when the component is destroyed. This removes the need to write manual cleanup code for that subscription.
interview.followUp: Why is this useful? It helps avoid subscriptions remaining active after their component is gone.

interview.question: How is AsyncPipe used in a template?
interview.answer: Use it in a template with the pipe operator, such as {{ value$ | async }}. The source can be an Observable or a Promise.
interview.followUp: What does the template receive before a value is available? The documented transform overload allows null, so the result can be null.

keyPoints: AsyncPipe turns an asynchronous source into the value that the template can display.
It supports both Observables and Promises and exposes the newest value from the source.
A new source value causes Angular to check the component for an updated view.
Component destruction triggers automatic unsubscription.
Replacing the source reference causes AsyncPipe to leave the old source and use the new one.
The pipe is available from Angular's CommonModule.
gotchas: Changing the input to a different Observable or Promise replaces the current subscription. The old one is unsubscribed automatically.

bootstrapApplication.summary: Starts an Angular application with a standalone root component. It returns a promise that resolves to an `ApplicationRef` and accepts optional application configuration.
bootstrapApplication.explanation: `bootstrapApplication` creates and starts an Angular application from a standalone root component. Pass an optional configuration object to add application providers, or use `importProvidersFrom` to include providers from an existing NgModule.
bootstrapApplication.syntax: bootstrapApplication(rootComponent: Type<unknown>, options?: ApplicationConfig, context?: BootstrapContext): Promise<ApplicationRef>

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: Optional application configuration, including providers for the application injector.

parameters.name: context
parameters.description: Optional context with a pre-existing platform injector. This can help with advanced cases such as server-side rendering.

example.explanation: This defines a standalone root component and starts the Angular application with it.

useCases.title: Bootstrap a standalone app
useCases.scenario: Starting a new Angular application with a standalone root component.

useCases.title: Configure providers
useCases.scenario: Adding application-wide services or values during startup.

useCases.title: Reuse NgModule providers
useCases.scenario: Using providers from an existing NgModule in a standalone application.

useCases.scenario: Creating applications during server-side rendering.

interview.question: What does `bootstrapApplication` do?
interview.answer: It starts an Angular application using a standalone root component and returns a promise. The promise resolves to an `ApplicationRef`.
interview.followUp: How would you add application-wide providers? Pass an object with a `providers` array as the second argument.

interview.question: How do you configure providers during bootstrap?
interview.answer: Use the second argument and provide application-level providers in its `providers` array. Each provider can define a token and its value or factory.
interview.followUp: How can an existing NgModule contribute providers? Add `importProvidersFrom(SomeNgModule)` to that array.

interview.question: Does bootstrapApplication include Testability?
interview.answer: The function does not include Testability by default. Add the providers returned by `provideProtractorTestingSupport()` when that support is needed.
interview.followUp: What is the related limitation for the root component? It must be standalone.

keyPoints: The function returns a promise. It resolves to an `ApplicationRef`.
Use the second argument to add providers to the application injector.
`importProvidersFrom` lets an existing NgModule and its imported modules supply providers.
An optional context can reuse a platform injector, which is useful for server-side rendering where a platform is created per request.
For new applications, Angular recommends this function instead of the older NgModule bootstrap method.
gotchas: The root component must be standalone. A non-standalone component cannot be passed as the root.
Testability is not added automatically. Add `provideProtractorTestingSupport()` when the application needs it.

Change detection.summary: Angular component metadata can control change detection, template whitespace, and validation of custom elements. OnPush performs fewer automatic checks, while schemas can allow elements that Angular does not recognize.
Change detection.explanation: A component's changeDetection setting controls when Angular checks its view. OnPush limits automatic checks to input changes from template bindings, events in the component, or an explicit mark-for-check call. Eager checks the component when Angular reaches it during traversal.

parameters.name: changeDetection
parameters.description: Selects the component's change detection mode. Supported values include ChangeDetectionStrategy.OnPush and ChangeDetectionStrategy.Eager.

parameters.name: preserveWhitespaces
parameters.description: When true, keeps otherwise unnecessary whitespace in the component template.

parameters.name: schemas
parameters.description: Lists schemas that change validation of elements and properties in the component template.

example.title: Use OnPush change detection
example.explanation: This component uses OnPush and updates its own view when its button event runs.

useCases.title: Reduce view checking
useCases.scenario: A component updates through signals, inputs, or local events and should avoid unnecessary checks.

useCases.title: Use custom elements
useCases.scenario: A template contains a web component that Angular does not know.

useCases.title: Preserve whitespace
useCases.scenario: Template formatting whitespace must remain in the rendered result.

interview.question: When does an OnPush component get checked?
interview.answer: OnPush is Angular's limited-checking mode. Angular checks the component when a template-bound input changes, an event listener in that component runs, or the component is marked for checking.
interview.followUp: What can mark an OnPush component for checking? ChangeDetectorRef.markForCheck can do it, and wrappers such as AsyncPipe can also mark it.

interview.question: How do you allow custom elements in a component template?
interview.answer: CUSTOM_ELEMENTS_SCHEMA allows a component template to use unknown custom elements. Add it to the component metadata's schemas array.
interview.followUp: How can a template allow unknown properties too? Use NO_ERRORS_SCHEMA, which allows any element and any property.

interview.question: How can a component preserve template whitespace?
interview.answer: Angular normally removes and collapses unnecessary whitespace from templates. Set preserveWhitespaces to true in the component metadata to keep it.
interview.followUp: What kind of whitespace does the default behavior commonly affect? Newlines and indentation are common sources.

keyPoints: Set changeDetection in @Component to choose how Angular checks the component.
OnPush checks after a template binding changes one of the component's inputs.
An event handled by the component can cause Angular to check an OnPush view.
Code can request an OnPush check with ChangeDetectorRef.markForCheck.
Angular checks host property bindings during change detection and updates the host element when they change.
gotchas: OnPush also affects all child directives, and a child cannot replace that strategy.
Angular removes and combines extra template whitespace unless preserveWhitespaces is set to true.
NO_ERRORS_SCHEMA is broader than CUSTOM_ELEMENTS_SCHEMA because it permits any element and property.

ChangeDetectorRef.summary: ChangeDetectorRef controls when Angular checks a component view. It supports OnPush updates, local checks, and attaching or detaching a view from the change-detection tree.
ChangeDetectorRef.explanation: ChangeDetectorRef lets a component control when Angular checks its view. You can mark an OnPush view for checking, remove it from the change-detection tree, check it and its children immediately, or attach it again.

example.title: Mark an OnPush component for checking
example.explanation: markForCheck() asks Angular to check this OnPush component again.

useCases.title: Request an OnPush check
useCases.scenario: An OnPush component changes state from a timer or another source that does not update an input or handle a view event.

useCases.title: Run local checks on a schedule
useCases.scenario: A frequently changing list should update only at selected times.

useCases.title: Pause and resume a view
useCases.scenario: A live-data component should stop and resume updates based on a condition.

interview.question: What does markForCheck() do?
interview.answer: markForCheck() flags an OnPush view so Angular can check it during a later change-detection run. It is useful when the component changed without an input update or view event.
interview.followUp: What happens if the view is detached? A detached view is still skipped, so use detectChanges() for a local check or reattach it first.

interview.question: When would you use detach()?
interview.answer: detach() removes the view from Angular's change-detection tree. The view stays unchecked until reattach() is called, or until detectChanges() performs a local check.
interview.followUp: Why combine detach() with detectChanges()? This limits checks to times chosen by the application, such as a timer interval.

interview.question: How is detectChanges() different from reattach()?
interview.answer: detectChanges() checks the current view and its child views immediately. It is commonly paired with detach() to run local change detection instead of waiting for the normal tree traversal.
interview.followUp: How can a component resume normal checking? Call reattach(), which adds the previously detached view back to the change-detection tree.

keyPoints: markForCheck() is useful for OnPush views when normal update triggers did not occur.
Input changes and events normally make a component eligible for another check.
detach() removes the view from the normal change-detection traversal.
detectChanges() performs an immediate check of the view and descendants.
reattach() restores normal participation after a view was detached.
A detached component can use scheduled detectChanges() calls to control its checking frequency.
gotchas: After detach(), Angular skips the view during normal change-detection runs.
markForCheck() does not make a detached view run; reattach it or call detectChanges().

Component.summary: @Component marks a class as an Angular component and supplies metadata for its template, selector, styles, dependencies, and runtime behavior. Components are the main UI building blocks in Angular.
Component.explanation: The Component decorator tells Angular how to create and use a class as a UI component. It connects the class to a template, selector, styles, inputs, outputs, providers, and other metadata. A component is a directive with a template, and only one component can match a template element.

parameters.description: Change-detection mode.

parameters.name: inputs

parameters.description: Data-bound input properties.

parameters.name: outputs
parameters.description: Event-bound output properties.

interview.question: What does the Component decorator do?
interview.answer: @Component marks a class as an Angular component and supplies metadata that controls its processing, creation, and runtime use. Unlike other directives, a component always has a template.
interview.followUp: How does a component differ from a directive? A component is a directive associated with a template, and only one component can be created for a template element.

interview.question: How does Angular use a component selector?
interview.answer: The selector is the CSS-like pattern Angular uses to find where the component should be created. Supported forms include element, class, attribute, attribute-value, :not(), and comma-separated selectors.
interview.followUp: Can a selector cross element boundaries? No. Angular allows directive selectors only when they match within one element boundary.

interview.question: What is the purpose of the imports option?
interview.answer: A standalone component can list template dependencies in imports. These dependencies may be standalone components, directives, pipes, or existing NgModules.
interview.followUp: What happens if an NgModule-declared component uses imports? Angular reports a compilation error because this option is limited to standalone components.

keyPoints: @Component marks a class as an Angular component.
Every component has a template, either inline or in a separate file.
For standalone components, imports declares what the template can use.
changeDetection selects how Angular checks the component for binding updates.
encapsulation controls whether component styles are scoped, global, or native Shadow DOM styles.
Standalone components can be imported directly by standalone components or NgModules.
gotchas: Do not set both templateUrl and template in the same component.
Use imports and schemas only with standalone components; using them on an NgModule-declared component causes a compilation error.
A template element cannot create multiple components.
Use Type<unknown> instead of Type<Component> when describing a component class.

computed.summary: `computed` creates a signal from a computation function. It returns a read-only derived signal with the computation's result.
computed.explanation: `computed` creates a read-only signal whose value comes from a function. The function can read other signals, and the computed signal derives its value from those reads.
computed.syntax: computed<T>(computation: () => T, options?: CreateComputedOptions<T> | undefined): Signal<T>

parameters.name: computation
parameters.description: A function that computes and returns a value of type `T`.

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: Optional settings for equality comparison and a debug name.

computed.returns: A `Signal<T>` containing the value produced by the computation.

example.title: Derived value with computed
example.explanation: The computed signal reads count and returns twice its value. When count changes, Angular updates doubleCount when it is read again.

useCases.title: Derived state
useCases.scenario: Derive a value from one or more signals, such as calculating a total from item signals.

useCases.title: Debugging signal state
useCases.scenario: Expose a named computed signal for easier inspection in Angular DevTools.

useCases.title: Custom value comparison
useCases.scenario: Use custom equality rules when deciding whether computed results are equal.

interview.question: What does Angular's `computed` function return?
interview.answer: `computed` takes a function that returns a value and returns a `Signal` of that value. The function is used to derive the signal's result.
interview.followUp: What can the options object contain? It can contain `equal` for value comparison and `debugName` for Angular DevTools.

interview.question: What are the arguments to `computed`?
interview.answer: The computation is passed as the first argument. The optional second argument is `CreateComputedOptions<T>`, which can configure equality and a debug name.
interview.followUp: Why might equality matter? A custom equality function can define when two computed results count as the same.

interview.question: What is the return type of `computed`?
interview.answer: The returned value is `Signal<T>`, so the result is a signal rather than a plain value. The generic type `T` is the type returned by the computation.
interview.followUp: How can a developer make the signal easier to inspect? Set `debugName` in the options object.

keyPoints: The function accepts a computation and an optional options object, then returns a signal.
The computation is a function with no required arguments that produces the computed value.
The options argument is optional and can be omitted.
The result is a signal containing a value of type `T`.
The options can define an equality function for comparing computed values.
The options can include a string name for the computed signal.
gotchas: If you provide `equal`, Angular uses it to decide whether a new computed value is equal to the previous value.
`debugName` helps identify the computed signal in Angular DevTools; it does not change the computed value.

Dependency injection.summary: Angular dependency injection supplies a class with values, functions, objects, or services from outside the class. Code provides dependencies, and components, directives, services, and factory functions can inject them when running in an injection context.
Dependency injection.explanation: Angular dependency injection lets a class receive the objects, values, functions, or services it needs from outside. Angular makes dependencies available through providers and retrieves them with inject, often in components, directives, services, or provider factory functions.

example.title: Inject a dependency in a component
example.explanation: The component asks Angular for HttpClient instead of creating it. Angular supplies the dependency in the component's injection context.

useCases.title: Reusable services
useCases.scenario: Share business logic or state between components and pages.

useCases.title: Configuration
useCases.scenario: Supply API URLs, feature flags, or other environment settings.

useCases.title: Factories
useCases.scenario: Create a value differently according to runtime conditions.

useCases.title: Testing
useCases.scenario: Replace real implementations with test doubles in unit tests.

interview.question: What is dependency injection in Angular?
interview.answer: Dependency injection supplies a class's required values or objects from outside the class. In Angular, code provides dependencies and classes request them, commonly with inject in a component, directive, or service.
interview.followUp: What is an injection context? It is a runtime situation where the current injector is available, such as a DI-created constructor, a field initializer, or a provider factory.

interview.question: What kinds of values can Angular inject?
interview.answer: A dependency can be any JavaScript value, including an object, function, or class instance. Common examples include configuration values, factories, and services.
interview.followUp: Why are services common? They package reusable functionality, shared state, data access, authentication, logging, or event handling for use across an application.

interview.question: Where can inject() be called?
interview.answer: The inject function can be used during construction of a class created by Angular and in field initializers of that class. It can also run in provider and injection-token factory functions.
interview.followUp: What must be checked before moving inject into a callback? Confirm that the callback executes inside an injection context; otherwise the current injector is unavailable.

keyPoints: DI helps organize shared code by giving classes their dependencies instead of making those dependencies internally.
Providers register values so Angular's DI system can make them available.
Injection retrieves a registered value for the code that needs it.
Injected dependencies may be configuration values, factory functions, or services.
Components and directives can both receive dependencies and make dependencies available.
Angular uses a runtime injection context to track the current injector while eligible code runs.
gotchas: Call inject only while Angular is running code in an injection context. Calling it later, outside that runtime context, does not work.
A service must use Angular's service decorator before it can be injected.

Directive.explanation: The Directive decorator marks a class as an Angular directive and supplies metadata for how Angular finds and creates it. A selector matches elements in a template, while inputs, outputs, providers, host bindings, and queries configure the directive. Directives are standalone by default; use standalone: false when declaring one in an NgModule.

interview.question: What does the Directive decorator do?
interview.answer: The decorator marks a class as a directive and provides metadata. Angular uses that metadata to match the directive, create its instance, and configure its behavior.
interview.followUp: How can a directive be made available outside its NgModule? Add it to the NgModule exports array, and ensure it is declared there and is not standalone.

interview.question: How does a directive selector work?
interview.answer: The selector tells Angular which template elements receive the directive. It can match an element, class, attribute, attribute value, a negated selector, or one of several comma-separated selectors.
interview.followUp: Can a selector cross from a parent element into a child element? No. Angular only permits selectors that stay within one element boundary.

interview.question: What is the default standalone behavior?
interview.answer: A directive is standalone unless its metadata sets standalone to false. Standalone directives can be used by other components without being declared in an NgModule.
interview.followUp: What must be done for an NgModule directive? Declare it in exactly one NgModule and export it when code outside that module must use it.

The selector controls where Angular creates the directive.
Inputs receive template-bound values and update during change detection.
Outputs expose directive events to template event handlers.
The host option binds directive members to host properties, attributes, and events.
Directives are standalone by default.
gotchas: A selector cannot match across element boundaries.
Do not declare a standalone directive in an NgModule.
An NgModule directive must be declared in exactly one NgModule.
A directive used through hostDirectives does not use its selector for that application.

effect.summary: Registers a function that runs when signals read by that function change. Angular creates either a component effect or a root effect, with different timing and change-detection behavior.
effect.explanation: effect() registers a function that Angular runs when the signals read by that function change. It can create a component effect or a root effect, depending on where it is called.
effect.syntax: effect(effectFn: (onCleanup: EffectCleanupRegisterFn) => void, options?: CreateEffectOptions | undefined): EffectRef;

parameters.name: effectFn
parameters.description: A callback that reads signals and can register cleanup work through onCleanup.

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: Optional settings for creating the effect.

example.explanation: The effect reads count, so Angular runs it again when count changes.

useCases.title: Component state reactions
useCases.scenario: A component needs to react to signal changes during Angular synchronization and may need to work with component state.

useCases.title: Root-level reactions
useCases.scenario: Code outside the component tree needs signal-driven work that runs independently as a microtask.

useCases.title: Register cleanup work
useCases.scenario: An effect starts work that must be cleaned up when the effect is disposed or rerun.

interview.question: What does Angular effect() do?
interview.answer: effect() registers a function that runs again when a signal read inside it changes. The function receives onCleanup, which can be used to register cleanup work.
interview.followUp: How do component and root effects differ? Component effects run during Angular synchronization and can interact with component state, while root effects run as microtasks without a component-tree or change-detection connection.

interview.question: What is a component effect?
interview.answer: A component effect is created from a component, directive, or one of their services. It runs as part of Angular's synchronization process, so it can safely read input signals or create and destroy views that depend on component state.
interview.followUp: What happens when the same code runs in a root service? It creates a root effect instead, and that effect runs as a microtask rather than as a component lifecycle event.

interview.question: What is a root effect?
interview.answer: A root effect is created outside the component tree, such as in a root service. It runs as a microtask and is not connected to the component tree or change detection.
interview.followUp: How can effect() work outside an injection context? Pass an injector manually in the effect options; otherwise the call must occur in an injection context.

keyPoints: Angular schedules the effect again when a signal read by the effect changes.
Angular has two effect types, and their execution timing depends on where the effect is created.
Component effects run during Angular synchronization, alongside the component lifecycle.
Component effects can read input signals and manage views that depend on component state.
Root effects run as microtasks and do not participate in the component tree or change detection.
The callback receives an onCleanup function for registering work to run when Angular cleans up the effect.
gotchas: Call effect() in an injection context, or provide an injector explicitly through its options.

ElementRef.explanation: ElementRef wraps an element from an Angular view. Its nativeElement property exposes the renderer-specific element, which is normally a DOM element in a browser. Use it only when Angular templates and data binding cannot solve the problem.

parameters.description: The render-specific element to wrap.

useCases.scenario: Code needs a browser-only DOM operation that Angular does not provide declaratively.

interview.question: What is ElementRef?
interview.answer: ElementRef is a wrapper around an element inside an Angular view. Its nativeElement property provides access to the renderer-specific element.
interview.followUp: What does nativeElement usually contain in a browser? It is usually a DOM element, but the type depends on the renderer.

interview.question: What does the ElementRef constructor receive?
interview.answer: The constructor accepts one value, nativeElement, whose type is the generic type T. The instance stores that value in its nativeElement property.
interview.followUp: How can the element type be made clearer? Use a generic such as ElementRef<HTMLButtonElement>.

interview.question: When should ElementRef be used?

interview.answer: inject() retrieves a dependency from Angular's injector using a provider token. It returns the injected value when the token can be resolved.
interview.followUp: What happens when the token is missing? With optional injection, inject() returns null; without optional injection, the lookup is not successful.

interview.question: Where can inject() be called?
interview.answer: Valid calls include field initializers, constructor bodies, and provider factories. These run while Angular is creating the class or resolving the factory.

A field initializer is a valid place to call inject().
A constructor body is a valid place to call inject().
Optional injection returns null when Angular cannot find the token.

interview.question: What does Angular's `input` function do?
interview.answer: `input` declares a signal-based component input. Angular updates the signal when the parent supplies a new bound value, and a template reads the current value by calling the signal.
interview.followUp: How do you require the parent to provide a value? Use `input.required<T>()`, which returns an input signal of type `T`.

interview.question: Which forms of `input` are available?
interview.answer: Use `input<T>()` when there is no initial value, `input(defaultValue)` when a default is useful, and `input.required<T>()` when the input must be supplied. The return type reflects whether `undefined` is possible.
interview.followUp: What happens when a transform is configured? Angular accepts the transform input type and stores the transformed result as type `T`.

interview.question: How can an input change or convert incoming values?
interview.answer: The options can include an alias and a transform. An alias changes the name used for binding in a template, while the transform converts the incoming value before the component uses it.
interview.followUp: Why can a transform have a different input type? This lets template values such as strings be converted into the component's desired type, such as a number or boolean.

interview.question: What does toObservable do?
interview.answer: toObservable takes a Signal<T> and returns an Observable<T>. The Observable exposes the signal's value and sends changes to subscribers through an effect.
interview.followUp: What happens when the signal changes several times quickly? Only the last value may be emitted if the effect has not run yet.

interview.question: What does a new subscriber receive?
interview.answer: A subscriber receives the latest signal value when it subscribes. This makes the Observable reflect the signal's current state rather than only future changes.
interview.followUp: Why is this different from subscribing to a plain event stream? A state-reflecting Observable supplies the current value to each new subscriber.

interview.question: When is an injector needed?
interview.answer: The function normally needs an injection context. If no such context is available, pass an injector in ToObservableOptions.
interview.followUp: What timing guarantee does the returned Observable provide? It is not guaranteed to be immediately synchronized with signal updates because the effect runs asynchronously.

keyPoints: It adapts an Angular Signal so RxJS code can consume it as an Observable.
Each new subscriber receives the signal's current value.
An Angular effect forwards signal values to the Observable's subscribers.
The source parameter is the Signal<T> that supplies values.
The optional options parameter can configure the conversion, including injector-related setup.
gotchas: Do not expect the Observable to emit at the exact moment the signal changes.
Several updates made before the effect runs may produce only one emission containing the final value.
Call it in an injection context, or provide an injector through the options.

interview.question: What does provideHttpClient do?
interview.answer: It registers HttpClient in the dependency-injection system and returns environment providers. Features passed to the function customize the client.
interview.followUp: How do you add interceptors? Use provideHttpClient(withInterceptors([...])). Functional interceptors are preferred over older DI-based interceptors.

interview.question: Which request backend does HttpClient use by default?
interview.answer: The default client uses the Fetch API. Add withXhr() when XMLHttpRequest behavior is required, but do not use it in SSR.
interview.followUp: What is one Fetch limitation mentioned by the guide? Fetch does not produce upload progress events.

interview.question: What does withRequestsMadeViaParent do?
interview.answer: A child HttpClient normally replaces the parent configuration. withRequestsMadeViaParent() makes child requests continue through the parent client after the child interceptors run.
interview.followUp: What must exist for this feature to work? An HttpClient instance must be configured above the current injector.

Route guards.summary: Angular route guards control whether navigation can enter or leave a route. They can allow navigation, block it, redirect it, or return an asynchronous result.
Route guards.explanation: A route guard is a function that controls navigation to or from a route. It can allow navigation, block it, or return a redirect; asynchronous guards use the first emitted result. Guards help with client-side navigation, but the server must also enforce authorization.
Route guards.syntax:
ng generate guard CUSTOM_NAME

{ path: 'dashboard', component: Dashboard, canActivate: [authGuard] }

parameters.description: The route snapshot being activated, including route-specific information; used by CanActivate.

parameters.name: state
parameters.description: The current router state; used by CanActivate.

parameters.name: route context
parameters.description: A route-specific service context and route information available to guards.

Route guards.returns: boolean; UrlTree or RedirectCommand; Promise<T>; or Observable<T>. The router uses the first emitted asynchronous value and then unsubscribes.

interview.question: What is a route guard?
interview.answer: A route guard controls whether navigation may continue. It can return true, false, a redirect value, or a Promise or Observable of one of those values.
interview.followUp: Which guard checks a route before activation? CanActivate. Which guard can select between routes with the same path? CanMatch.

interview.question: What are the main guard types?
interview.answer: CanActivate checks access to one route. CanActivateChild applies a check to the child routes under a route. CanDeactivate checks whether the current component may be left.
interview.followUp: When would CanDeactivate be useful? Use it to stop leaving a page with unsaved changes.

interview.question: How does Angular handle multiple guards?
interview.answer: Guards are listed in route configuration arrays. Navigation proceeds only when every guard returns true; otherwise the router uses the first non-true result according to array order.
interview.followUp: Can guards provide security by themselves? No. Server-side authorization is still required because browser code can be modified.

keyPoints: Use guards to check entry to a route or departure from it.
A boolean result directly allows or blocks navigation.
Return a UrlTree or RedirectCommand when navigation should go to another route.

The documented guard types are CanActivate, CanActivateChild, CanDeactivate, and CanMatch.

gotchas: A browser user can change JavaScript, so enforce authorization on the server as well.
Guards in one array can run concurrently. Do not make one asynchronous guard depend on work from an earlier guard.
A false result from CanMatch can make the router try another route instead of stopping navigation.

interview.question: What makes a component standalone?
interview.answer: A standalone component does not need to be declared in an NgModule. It can be imported directly by another standalone component or by an NgModule.
interview.followUp: How does its template get access to dependencies? The component lists those dependencies in its imports metadata.

interview.question: What belongs in a standalone component's imports array?
interview.answer: The imports array contains the template dependencies, such as standalone components, directives, pipes, and existing NgModules. Angular uses this list to make them available in the component template.
interview.followUp: Can an imports entry be an NgModule? Yes. Standalone components can import existing NgModules as well as standalone declarations.

interview.question: Why use standalone components in an existing application?
interview.answer: Standalone components provide a simpler authoring model by reducing the need for NgModules. Existing applications can adopt the style incrementally.

toSignal.summary: Converts an RxJS Observable into an Angular Signal. The signal always exposes the latest emitted value and can clean up its subscription with the Angular injection context.
toSignal.explanation: toSignal subscribes to an Observable and exposes its latest emitted value through a synchronous Angular Signal. It throws if the Observable errors. Angular normally destroys the subscription with the current injection context; an Injector can provide cleanup, or manualCleanup can keep the subscription until the Observable completes.

interview.question: How does toSignal convert an Observable?
interview.answer: toSignal subscribes to the Observable and returns a Signal containing its newest value. The signal can be read synchronously, and it throws when the Observable errors.
interview.followUp: What happens before the first emission? The signal needs either an initialValue, or requireSync: true for an Observable that emits immediately; without either, its type can include undefined.

interview.question: How is the subscription cleaned up?
interview.answer: By default, Angular uses a DestroyRef from the current injection context to clean up the subscription when that context is destroyed. An Injector option can supply the cleanup context explicitly.
interview.followUp: How can cleanup be disabled? Set manualCleanup so DestroyRef is not used; the subscription then lasts until the Observable completes.

interview.question: What does requireSync do?
interview.answer: requireSync: true asserts that the Observable emits immediately when subscribed. It removes the need for an initial value and gives the returned signal a type without undefined.
interview.followUp: What is the trade-off? A non-synchronous Observable causes a runtime error when the signal is created, so an initialValue is safer when immediate emission is not guaranteed.

keyPoints: Use toSignal when Angular code needs synchronous signal access to values produced by an Observable.
After each emission, reading the signal returns that newest value.
An Observable error is not converted into a normal signal value; reading or using the signal can throw.
requireSync: true avoids both an initial value and undefined in the signal type when immediate emission is guaranteed.
The default lifecycle is automatic cleanup when the context that created the signal is destroyed.
gotchas: Use requireSync only when the Observable always emits during subscription. Otherwise, signal creation throws at runtime.
Calling toSignal outside an injection context needs an Injector, unless manualCleanup is enabled.
manualCleanup leaves the subscription active until the Observable completes, so use it only when that lifetime is intended.
